about: The estate's core principles, in ONE place (doc 95, section 8). Every app built from the OS kit carries the core ones automatically and may add others; an edition may say a principle in its own words but cannot drop a core one. Change a principle here and ./securax os check fails until every app is rebuilt with it (./securax os build --all), so a better principle reaches every app. AGENTS.md section 0 holds the same north star for builders.
north_star: The person or team using it is visibly better off: better work, better decisions, a calmer and more purposeful life, risks really reduced. Not paperwork.

principles.name: Ikigai
principles.text: Work where what you love, what you are good at, what you are valued for and what the world needs meet; it keeps you going for years, not weeks.

principles.name: Antifragility
principles.text: Every failure leaves a lesson, a change and a drill, so the next stress finds you stronger.

principles.name: Start as an amoeba, carry the DNA
principles.text: Ship the simplest living thing that helps today — one person, no server, offline — but carry the full blueprint inside it, and build the dormant seam (the rail) that lets each part grow into its enterprise form. Nature is the architect: a cell becomes an organism only as conditions call for it. So the estate senses its own conditions — favourable (more nodes, more teams, traffic north-south and east-west, spare resources) and unfavourable (load, failure, a lost node) — and grows the next form when they warrant it: the safe, in-box steps by itself, the ones that provision or cost or touch endpoints behind a human's approval. Never build the organism before the amoeba is alive and used; never ship an amoeba with no DNA to become the organism.

principles.name: One door, no passwords
principles.text: Sign in once, with an account you already have (a passkey, Microsoft or Google), and that is the only door. Everything else a person reaches, a cloud, a mailbox, a drive, a new app, comes through that one sign-in, asks for a permission only at the moment it is needed, takes the smallest one, and is taken away in one place. Everything works as a guest first, with nothing to sign in to for the basics; signing in adds sync, an allowance and services. A feature never builds its own login screen or keeps a password: it declares what it needs in governance/identity.json and the one door does the rest.

principles.name: Built for the largest organisations
principles.text: Every component is designed as if for the largest organisations from its first line. Before and after every change, look for what stops if one machine, host, account, key or person is gone; any login or step a person must repeat; anything that looks or works badly in either theme, on a phone, offline or by keyboard; any gap in security and privacy; and anything that cannot be seen, recovered or taken away. Fix the cheap findings now, date the rest in the queue, and say plainly what was not tested.

principles.name: Think like the attacker first
principles.text: Before you build anything that crosses a trust boundary, model it as the attacker would: its parts, its data flows and where trust changes, and what could go wrong for each part in all six STRIDE ways (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege). Each threat is mitigated with proof, accepted with a reason and a review date, or ruled out with a reason. Draw it in any tool you like (the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, OWASP Threat Dragon, a whiteboard); the repository keeps it as plain text in governance/threat-models.json, and the checks hold it to account.

principles.name: Small wins, shown
principles.text: Progress you can see keeps you going; the app shows it every week.

principles.name: Least effort for you
principles.text: The app does the remembering, the checking and the reminding; you do the one next step.

principles.name: Calm by default
principles.text: When all is well the screen is quiet. Only what needs you lights up, with why it matters and the one thing to do; everything else waits one tap away.

principles.name: No manual needed
principles.text: Anyone can use it the first time, on a phone or a laptop, by keyboard or screen reader, in light or dark. If it needs explaining, it is not finished.

principles.name: Built for a human mind
principles.text: People judge it in seconds by how it looks, and stay for how it feels to use: fast, few steps, nothing to learn, nothing that nags. Invite, never command, because pressure makes people push back; make the right choice the easy default; end every visit on a small win. Never trick anyone.

principles.name: See the whole
principles.text: Start from what the person needs, not from what exists. Question every requirement, delete before adding, simplify, then speed up and automate. Weigh look, feel, engineering, safety and cost together, and finish the parts no one sees as carefully as the parts everyone does.

principles.name: A system lives in the calendar
principles.text: Every step that repeats goes into your own calendar in one tap, with what to do written inside, so the system runs without you remembering it. Each event keeps its identity for ever: a newer version updates it in place, and a step that ends is ended cleanly, so no change ever clashes with what you already have.

principles.name: Built for the world, at home in one place
principles.text: Every word a person reads comes from a catalog, every number, date and currency is formatted for their region, and every layout also works right to left. One tap chooses Local (one country's rules, money and language) or Global (content that assumes no country, in the person's own language); content that is true in one country only is tagged, and never shown in Global. A language stays beta until a native speaker has reviewed it, and nothing private ever goes to a translator.

principles.name: One open action
principles.text: When many things compete, work on one at a time, and let the system choose it by risk: the lowest unfinished layer first, then risk times reach divided by effort. Show that one plainly, with its one button; fold everything else under Later until it is done, and offer the vital few when a list is long. Focus is the method; the next one moves up by itself.

principles.name: Build the system, not the goal
principles.text: Results come from systems, not willpower. For every outcome, build the loop that makes it happen by itself: a cue at the right moment, the smallest step that still counts, a reward you can see, a calendar that remembers for you, and a regular review that improves the loop. Find the one constraint that limits the whole loop and remove it first.

principles.name: Pareto
principles.text: A few actions carry most of the result. Find them first.

principles.name: Inversion
principles.text: Ask what could ruin it, and remove that downside before chasing upside.

principles.name: Control the inputs
principles.text: You cannot control outcomes. You control decisions, rhythm and follow-through.

principles.name: Compounding
principles.text: A small review kept every week for a year beats a perfect plan kept for a month.

principles.name: Flywheel
principles.text: Each improvement makes the next one easier: visibility earns trust, trust earns support, support builds capability.

principles.name: Never miss twice
principles.text: Missing once is life. Missing twice is the start of a new habit, so the floor is two minutes.

principles.name: Best choice, pre-made
principles.text: Offer the fewest, best options and pre-select the best one. Never a blank field or a wall of equal choices; the right path is the obvious, already-made choice, one tap away.

principles.name: Shape the environment, not the person
principles.text: Change the setting, not the willpower. Make the good path automatic and the harmful path effortful, with a one-time set-up the environment then enforces — never a rule the person must remember to follow.

principles.name: Built for the worst day
principles.text: Assume the person is distracted, overwhelmed, out of willpower and short on skill, and still make success the default. Build for them and it works for everyone.

principles.name: Aim at success, not only safety
principles.text: Design for the win the person wants, not only the disaster to avoid. Every safeguard also moves them forward; a control that prevents harm but advances nothing is not finished.

principles.name: Choose who you serve
principles.text: Design each product for one clearly-named best-fit person and serve them completely, with an honest self-selection mechanic — a fair price, a fit signal — that draws them in and gently turns the wrong fit away; never chase volume that dilutes the fit. Run a barbell: a high margin from a chosen few funds a low-friction, low-cost-to-serve many, markets taken in order of who pays most for the least cost to serve — while the free safety core stays free for everyone and the mechanic is never a dark pattern or a denial of safety.
